summary: Draft watchdog-family record. `Win32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds` sits under `HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Power`, is absent by default on the observed clean baseline, has a current-build Unicode string hit in `ntoskrnl.exe`, and now has direct KVM local-KD proof that the running kernel keeps `nt!PopWin32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds = 30` and consumes that global in `nt!PopInvokeWin32CalloutWithWatchdog` by multiplying it by `1000` before issuing the watchdog packet through `ZwPowerInformation`. This is a stronger current-build lead than the bugcheck-enabled sibling, but the exact registry seeding path and non-default override semantics are still unproven.

setting.name: Win32k Callout Watchdog Timeout Seconds
setting.casual_explanation: This appears to be a low-level power-manager watchdog timeout for Win32k callouts. On the observed clean baseline the registry value is not configured, but the running kernel still keeps an in-memory default.
setting.why_people_change_it: Kernel and power researchers may inspect this value when tracing Win32k callout watchdog behavior and watchdog packet timing in the power manager.
setting.tradeoffs_overview: The value is kernel-adjacent, not user-facing, and only partially understood. Current-build usage is real and direct, but the exact registry seeding path and safe non-default semantics are still missing.
setting.professional_notes: The repo docs-first power routing pass already listed `HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Power\\Win32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds` as a new candidate. A later existence-first pass on the observed clean baseline confirmed that the `Control\\Power` path exists while the value itself is absent. A later targeted current-build string batch found an exact Unicode hit for `Win32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds` in `C:\\Windows\\System32\\ntoskrnl.exe`. A later KVM local-KD follow-up then resolved the live current-build watchdog-family cluster around `PopInvokeWin32CalloutWithWatchdog` and directly read `PopWin32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds = 0x1e` (`30`). The same pass disassembled `PopInvokeWin32CalloutWithWatchdog` and showed a direct `imul` against the global by `1000`, followed by the watchdog packet path through `ZwPowerInformation` and the surrounding Win32 callout path. That is materially stronger than a string-only or sibling-only clue: the running kernel is actively consuming the global even though the registry value is missing on the observed baseline. The main open question is whether the registry value is an optional override on top of a built-in 30-second default, or whether a boot-only helper still seeds the same global from `Control\\Power` when present.

evidence.summary: A live KVM local-KD pass read `PopWin32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds = 30` and disassembled `PopInvokeWin32CalloutWithWatchdog`, which directly multiplies the global by `1000` before issuing the watchdog packet through `ZwPowerInformation` and then returning to `PsInvokeWin32Callout`.

decision.why: The candidate is strong enough for a schema-backed draft because the path/value clue, current-build string hit, and direct current-build caller consumption are all real. It is not ready for a validated record because the exact registry seeding path, non-default override semantics, and safe rollback behavior for a present value are still unproven.

Which power-manager helper seeds `PopWin32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds` when the registry value is present, if any?
Does changing the value alter only the `ZwPowerInformation` watchdog packet timeout, or are there additional sibling code paths that consume the same global?
